risk.title: So you hand over the phone
risk.body: A child who won’t open a paper dictionary will happily type into a search box. Then come image results, videos and adverts that were never made for them. In a 2022 survey of American teenagers, 15% said they first saw pornography online at 10 or younger, and 58% of those who had seen it said they had come across it by accident. Gloss is the screen you can hand over instead: 65,019 words checked for children, no adverts, no web results, and it shows you how to lock the tablet to Gloss with the phone’s own Guided Access or screen pinning.

citations.label: Common Sense Media, Teens and Pornography (survey of 1,358 US teens aged 13–17, September 2022)

dictionary.title: Dictionaries were made for grown-ups
dictionary.body: The first English dictionary, Robert Cawdrey’s Table Alphabeticall of 1604, explained “hard usual English words” to adult readers. Dictionaries written for children came much later — the Thorndike-Century Junior Dictionary of 1935, built on a count of the words children actually meet, is one of the best known — and they made the words simpler. The form stayed the same: a list of written definitions, at one level, for everybody. Our own children, and their friends, didn’t open it. This is what changes when a dictionary is built for a child from the start.

citations.label: Cawdrey’s Table Alphabeticall (1604), University of Toronto notes on early English dictionaries
The Thorndike-Century Junior Dictionary (1935), Indiana University Lilly Library

pictures.title: A picture isn’t a shortcut
pictures.body: People remember pictures better than words — psychologists call it the picture superiority effect. One explanation, Allan Paivio’s dual coding, is that a word with a picture is stored twice: once as language and once as an image. But it has to be the right picture. Search “bat” and cricket bats and animals arrive together; search an innocent word and you can’t know what comes back. In Gloss each picture belongs to one meaning and is checked before it ships. 1,200 words have one today; this campaign pays for 5,000.

citations.label: The picture superiority effect, with references to Paivio’s dual-coding research

depths.title: Easy explanations, and the hard ones too
depths.body: Simple, More, Deeper and All: the same meaning written four ways. A seven-year-old who finds reading hard starts at Simple. A confident eleven-year-old opens All and meets the full grown-up definition, safely. Every child starts where they are and steps up when they are ready — that is how the muscle builds.

dictionary.title: Dictionaries were made for grown-ups
dictionary.body: Noah Webster’s American Dictionary of 1828 was written for adults, like the English dictionaries before it. Dictionaries written for kids came a century later — the Thorndike-Century Junior Dictionary of 1935, built on a count of the words kids actually meet and a fixture of American classrooms for decades, is one of the best known — and they made the words simpler. The form stayed the same: a list of written definitions, at one level, for everybody. Our own kids, and their friends, didn’t open it. This is what changes when a dictionary is built for a kid from the start.

languages.name: Hinglish
languages.who: For families who speak Hindi, in India and around the world
languages.promise: English words from your child’s books, explained the way your family talks, with the Hindi word beside them.
languages.roots: Your child reads “uncle” at school. At home there’s chacha, mama, tau, and more. Gloss shows the English word and the Hindi ones together, so the words from Dadi’s house aren’t lost to a school book.
languages.forFun: A child in Leeds whose best friend speaks Hindi can tap “duck”, see बतख़, read it as batakh, and hear it said by a Hindi voice. One new word a day, for fun.
languages.builtIntro: Hindi already works in Gloss, on a small set of test words. This is what it does today:

built.title: The Hindi word, beside the English one
built.body: Open “duck” and a Hindi chip shows बतख़. Tap it for the Hindi page, written in Devanagari with Roman spelling (batakh).

built.title: Said by a Hindi voice
built.body: बतख़ is said in Hindi and duck in English, from recordings stored on the phone, so they play offline.

built.title: Words English doesn’t have
built.body: “Uncle” shows five Hindi words, each saying which uncle: चाचा, मामा and more. जुगाड़ gets an explanation, because English has no word for it.

costReference.built: We built British English first: 65,019 words checked for children, nearly every word spoken, 63,265 words suggested offline, and 1,200 pictures.

readingEvidence.method: We took ten children’s novels anyone can read for free — Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Peter Pan, The Secret Garden, The Jungle Book, Black Beauty, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Railway Children, Anne of Green Gables, Pollyanna and The Wind in the Willows — cut each into chapters of 2,500 words, and counted the words in each chapter that most children learn only after a given age.
notes: To follow a story on your own, you need to know about 98% of its words; at 95% there is a stranger every 20 words (Hu & Nation, 2000).

The middle child in a study of ten- and eleven-year-olds read books for 4.6 minutes a day — about 282,000 words a year. The child at the top tenth read 21.1 minutes, about 1.8 million words (Anderson, Wilson & Fielding, 1988).
Our own rough sum: 282,000 words is about 113 chapters, and at {unknownWordsAt9} new words a chapter that is some 5,000 times a year a child stops at a word.
readingEvidence.caveat: Each number is the middle book; the range is the easiest and the hardest. These are older books, and modern ones may have fewer hard words. The ages are adults’ ratings of when they learned each word, so they are averages, not tests of your child. Names are not counted, and a word counts once per chapter.

citations.label: Kuperman, Stadthagen-González & Brysbaert (2012), age-of-acquisition ratings for 30,000 English words
Hu & Nation (2000) on 98% coverage, summarised in a replication study
Anderson, Wilson & Fielding (1988), Reading Research Quarterly 23 — table via Corwin
